Lighthouses have guarded dangerous coastlines for thousands of years, standing as tall, sturdy beacons that guide sailors away from rocks and toward safe harbors. The earliest known example, the Pharos of Alexandria, was built in the third century BC and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Over the centuries, builders learned to craft towers that could withstand relentless waves, fierce winds, and the isolation of remote headlands and reefs.

Early lighthouses relied on open fires, then candles and oil lamps, with mirrors used to amplify the glow. A major leap came in the 1820s with Augustin Fresnel's lens, which used concentric rings of glass prisms to focus light into a powerful beam visible for many miles. Each lighthouse also developed its own signature pattern of flashes, so mariners could identify exactly which light they were seeing and confirm their position.

Today, GPS and electronic charts have made lighthouses less essential for navigation, and many have been automated or decommissioned. Yet they remain beloved symbols of resilience, solitude, and guidance.
